lines.text: In December twenty twenty-three, a computer closed Rotterdam's door to the sea, and no human gave the order.
Storm Pia was driving the North Sea at the Dutch coast,
and the shipping channel to Rotterdam opens straight onto that sea, three hundred and sixty metres wide.
You see, every storm flood has two parts.
The tide rises on schedule, twice a day.
Then the wind piles extra water on top: the surge.
So the Dutch water agency handed the decision to a computer called BOS.
If it forecasts three metres above sea level at Rotterdam, it closes the barrier itself.
That evening, the forecast crossed the line.
Ships were halted, and the dry docks flooded.
Two hollow gates, each two hundred and ten metres long, swung out on ball joints ten metres wide.
The whole closing takes about two hours.
Then the gates filled with water and sank, sealing the channel.
That night, all six of the country's big storm barriers were shut.
About one and a half million people live behind this one, and not one of them had to press a button.
